# MCP-upstream config (v1)

Schema for `.tera/mcp-upstreams/<name>.hcl` config files. Each decodes to `pkg/config.MCPUpstreamBlock` (ADR-062) registering a server the gateway serves, exactly once. The block label is the registration name.

Two types. `type = "upstream"` (the default) is a **fronted** far-side MCP server reached over a transport — HTTP, sandboxed resident stdio, or HTTP over a unix socket (`transport = "unix"`, ADR-140 D9) — aggregated and fronted with far-side credential injection, and by default projected into the capability registry as `<name>.<tool>` tools (ADR-070 §3–§4). `type = "virtual"` is a **virtual MCP server**: no transport, no far-side URL, backed instead by the tool `capability_group` named in `group`, whose members may be locally declared tools, agents, or `<upstreamID>.<tool>` tools projected from the fronted upstreams above — one server composed from any tools the deployment can reach (ADR-062 §2 as amended). A virtual registration never projects (its members already are capabilities). Either type is exposed to clients the same way, through an `mcp_exposure`; a client cannot tell them apart.

The `health_check` block is what produces liveness signal, and nothing else does. An upstream that declares one is probed on that interval; its state drives circuit-breaking and endpoint failover (ADR-062 §5), and — since ADR-070 §6 — marks this upstream's projected tools as degraded (`io.kottera/degraded`, with the reason `upstream "<name>" unreachable`) wherever they appear as members of a `capability_group` served as a virtual MCP server. An upstream that declares **no** `health_check` block is never probed and therefore contributes no liveness signal at all: its projected members keep listing as healthy while it is down, and the failure surfaces only at call time. Degradation marks the listing but never refuses the call — a probe is sampled state, and refusing on a stale one would deny a recovered upstream.

## Example

A minimal `mcp-upstreams`: every required attribute, exactly one member of each closed union, and nothing optional beyond what the kind would otherwise render empty. It is generated from the same source these tables are, and the same bytes are run through `tera validate` by the ADR-087 D9 pattern-transfer test — so it cannot describe a shape the loader does not accept.

Cross-references name the other kinds' examples (`example-worker`, `example-tool`, …) because every kind's example is validated together with the rest, as one vault.

`.tera/mcp-upstreams/example-mcp-upstream.hcl`:

```hcl
version = "v1"

mcp_upstream "example-mcp-upstream" {
  endpoint = "https://example.internal"
}
```

## `materialization` block

| Attribute | Type | Required | Default | Since | Constraints | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `enabled` | boolean | no | — | — | — | Tri-state. Unset is auto: materialization is on iff this upstream advertises the io.modelcontextprotocol/tasks extension, and structurally off otherwise — the golden path, since the lossless route should not have to be found. false is the off switch: a "task" result from this upstream refuses by name instead of becoming a wrapper Work Order. true is an assertion about the far side, not an override of it — materialization stays off for an upstream that serves no tasks, and the mistake is reported as a warning naming the upstream at detection time rather than failing the boot, because the upstream may be down when the daemon starts. Turning materialization off on the only such upstream also removes the tasks extension from the advertisement of every exposure fronting it. |
| `poll_interval` | string | no | — | — | — | How often the tracking feed polls this upstream for its tasks' state, as a Go duration ("45s", "2m"). Applies only to the poll branch — an upstream that serves subscriptions/listen is followed by one stream instead. Omit for the profile-keyed default: 30s under server/gateway, 15s under embedded/desktop, 5s under dev, or the far side's own pollIntervalMs hint where it sent one (clamped to the profile's floor and to a quarter of the lost-contact window). An operator value is honoured verbatim rather than clamped, so a value below the one-second floor is refused by tera validate rather than silently raised. This is per-upstream because cadence is a property of the far side; the lost-contact timeout it is clamped against is deployment-shaped and stays profile-keyed with no per-upstream override. |

## `auth_far_side` block

| Attribute | Type | Required | Default | Since | Constraints | Description |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| `type` | string | yes | — | — | — | The far-side scheme: bearer or oauth (service modes, one credential the gateway holds for every caller), or connection (each caller's own credential, selected from the delegated-token vault by the connection named below). The retired per-person spellings user_delegated and user_token no longer load (ADR-148 D2; see docs/ops/upgrade-to-connections.md). |
| `connection` | string | no | — | — | — | Required for type = connection, refused otherwise: the .tera/connections/<name>.hcl this upstream acts through. The connection declares how a person obtains the credential - by consent through its oauth block, by pasting through its token block, or either - so the upstream carries no registration of its own. Several upstreams may name one connection; a person who connected it once is attached on all of them. |
| `authorization_server` | string | no | — | — | — | Retired: never valid. An inline per-person OAuth registration is refused at load naming ADR-148 D2 and docs/ops/upgrade-to-connections.md; declare it on a connection's oauth block instead. |
